noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to explain: i the trends in melting and boiling temperatures of the elements of Periods 2 and 3 of the Periodic Table in terms of the structure of the element and the bonding between its atoms or molecules ii the general increase and the specific trends in ionisation energy of the elements across Periods 2 and 3 of the Periodic Table iii the decrease in first ionisation energy down a group

primer.text: Melting points of the period 3 elements trace the bonding underneath them: metals climb from sodium to aluminium as each atom donates more electrons into the delocalised sea, silicon peaks on its giant covalent network, then phosphorus to argon collapse onto weak forces between simple molecules. This note walks the profile and the structures that force it.

lessons.title: Reading the period-3 melting profile
sourceHeadings: Melting Points of the Elements Across Period 3 Table
lessons.opening: Plot the melting points of the period 3 elements and one shape appears in both periods 2 and 3: values rise from sodium to a peak at silicon, then tumble through the non-metals to argon. The profile is not a property trend like radius - it is a structural story, told by metallic lattices, one giant covalent network and a run of simple molecules.
keyPoints: Period 2 and period 3 elements follow the same melting-point pattern.
Melting points climb from sodium up to silicon, which holds the highest value.
After silicon the values fall away sharply through phosphorus to argon.
The shape tracks bonding: metallic to the left, giant covalent at silicon, molecular to the right.
Sulfur melts above phosphorus because its S8 molecules outweigh the P4 units.

low.restatement: Melting points rise across the metals, hit their top at silicon, then sink steadily as the elements turn into small molecules.
low.analogy: A hill walk: the ascent gets steeper through three metallic towns, the summit is a silicon monastery, and the descent to argon is a scree slope of crumbling pebbles.
low.examPointer: Naming silicon as the peak is the free mark; misplacing the peak costs the whole profile question.

medium.restatement: Melting point reports the energy needed to dismantle a structure, so the period-3 curve is really a map of lattice strength: three metallic lattices of rising strength, one covalent network, then four molecular solids held by weak intermolecular forces.
medium.analogy: Compare demolition jobs: welded steel frames (metals) resist longer than a bolted glass dome (silicon), while stacked foam blocks (molecular solids) fall at a nudge.
medium.examPointer: Examiners want structure named per region - say 'giant metallic lattice', 'giant covalent network' and 'simple molecular' in the right order.

check.stem: Which period 3 element has the highest melting point?

options.text: Silicon
options.explanation: Its giant covalent network of strong bonds demands the most energy to break.

options.text: Aluminium
options.explanation: Aluminium tops the metals but sits below silicon's network.

options.text: Sodium
options.explanation: Sodium anchors the low end of the metallic climb.

options.text: Argon
options.explanation: Argon sits at the bottom of the descent, a lone simple atom.

check.stem: What happens to melting points after silicon across period 3?

options.text: They decrease significantly through the non-metals
options.explanation: Simple molecules shed easily, so values tumble after the network peak.

options.text: They continue rising to argon
options.explanation: The rise ends at silicon; everything after falls.

options.text: They hold level through phosphorus and sulfur
options.explanation: Only a modest sulfur bump above phosphorus interrupts the fall.

options.text: They collapse instantly to zero
options.explanation: The values fall but never reach zero.

check.stem: How do periods 2 and 3 compare in melting-point behaviour?

options.text: Both periods follow the same overall pattern
options.explanation: Rise to a group-14 peak, then fall through molecular elements, in either period.

options.text: Only period 3 shows a peak
options.explanation: Period 2 peaks at carbon in the same way.

options.text: The periods run in opposite directions
options.explanation: The profiles match, they do not mirror.

options.text: Melting points are random across both periods
options.explanation: The pattern is systematic and explainable by structure.

check.stem: Which region of period 3 accounts for the climb from sodium to aluminium?

options.text: Giant metallic lattices whose bonding strengthens with donated electrons
options.explanation: Each metal donates more valence electrons, tightening the lattice.

options.text: Giant covalent networks growing longer
options.explanation: A covalent network appears only at silicon.

options.text: Simple molecules of increasing size
options.explanation: Molecular elements sit after silicon and melt lower.

options.text: Falling atomic radii squeezing atoms together
options.explanation: Radius shrinkage is not the mechanism cited for the metallic climb.

check.stem: Sulfur melts at a higher temperature than phosphorus. What structural difference explains it?

options.text: Sulfur forms larger S8 molecules against phosphorus's smaller P4 units
options.explanation: Bigger molecules mean stronger intermolecular attractions to overcome.

options.text: Sulfur's covalent bonds break while phosphorus's survive
options.explanation: In both elements the covalent bonds stay intact on melting; only intermolecular forces give way.

options.text: Sulfur is metallic and phosphorus is not
options.explanation: Both are simple molecular non-metals.

options.text: Phosphorus has no covalent bonds at all
options.explanation: Within P4 the atoms are covalently bonded.

check.stem: State the melting-point profile of the period 3 elements from sodium to argon.
check.modelAnswer: Values rise from sodium to a maximum at silicon, then decrease significantly through phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon.

check.stem: Name the structural class of each of the three regions of the period-3 profile.
check.modelAnswer: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are giant metallic lattices; silicon is a giant covalent network; phosphorus to argon are simple molecular elements.

check.stem: Explain why the same melting-point pattern repeats in both period 2 and period 3.
check.modelAnswer: Both periods run metal, then one group-14 network former, then non-metals that exist as simple molecules, so the sequence metallic lattice, covalent network, molecular solid - and therefore the melting profile - repeats.

check.stem: Arrange sodium, silicon, sulfur and argon in order of decreasing melting point and label the structure responsible at each position.
check.modelAnswer: Silicon first (giant covalent network), then sodium (giant metallic lattice), then sulfur (S8 simple molecules), then argon (single atoms) - network beats metal beats molecular.

lessons.title: Structures behind the profile
sourceHeadings: Bonding & Structure of the Elements Table
lessons.opening: Every step of the period-3 melting profile is forced by structure. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium park positive ions in a giant lattice bathed by delocalised valence electrons; silicon wires every atom to its neighbours with strong covalent bonds; phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon exist as compact molecules where only weak intermolecular forces hold the solid together.
keyPoints: Na, Mg and Al are metallic: positive ions in a giant lattice held by a sea of delocalised electrons.
Valence-shell electrons fill the delocalised sea: one from Na, two from Mg, three from Al.
Aluminium bonds strongest of the three because its 3+ core and larger electron sea attract more.
Silicon melts highest because strong covalent bonds run through its whole giant network.
P4, S8, Cl2 and single-atom Ar melt easily: only weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces sit between molecules.

low.restatement: Metals melt at middling temperatures because ion-and-electron lattices take real effort to rearrange, silicon takes the most because its covalent grid must be broken, and molecular elements melt easily because molecules part without breaking bonds.
low.analogy: Unstacking magnetised balls (metal), sawing a welded frame (silicon), or sliding two Velcro tabs apart (molecules) - three increasing, then decreasing levels of effort.
low.examPointer: Draw the metallic lattice with rows of tightly packed positive ions; gaps or random scatter read as a liquid and lose marks.

medium.restatement: The melting order is an electrostatic ledger: Na gives one electron per atom to the sea, Mg two, Al three, so metallic attraction deepens left to right; silicon's network costs full covalent bonds; molecular solids only pay intermolecular change.
medium.analogy: Three glue dots, one welded seam, then a row of paperclips: the period ranks its solids by what must be undone to set them flowing.
medium.examPointer: State explicitly that covalent bonds within P4 or S8 survive melting - conflating intramolecular and intermolecular strength is the classic error.

check.stem: How many electrons does one aluminium atom donate to the delocalised sea?

options.text: Three
options.explanation: Aluminium's three valence electrons join the sea, the most of the three metals.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One donation belongs to sodium.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two donations belong to magnesium.

options.text: Four
options.explanation: Silicon, not aluminium, engages four electrons - covalently.

check.stem: Why is metallic bonding in aluminium stronger than in sodium?

options.text: A 3+ ion paired with more delocalised electrons draws harder than a 1+ ion with fewer
options.explanation: More charge and more sea electrons mean larger electrostatic forces.

options.text: Aluminium's ions are larger and overlap more
options.explanation: Its ions are not larger; the argument is charge and electron count.

options.text: Aluminium atoms share covalent bonds
options.explanation: The bonding is metallic, not covalent.

options.text: Sodium's lattice contains gaps
options.explanation: Sodium's lattice is regular; its bonding is just weaker.

check.stem: What must be overcome to melt silicon?

options.text: Strong covalent bonds running through the giant network
options.explanation: Melting the network means breaking the bonds that wire every atom to its neighbours.

options.text: Weak forces between small molecules
options.explanation: Silicon is not molecular; there are no separate molecules.

options.text: Electrostatic pull between ions and a delocalised sea
options.explanation: That is the metallic picture, not silicon's.

options.text: Nothing beyond van der Waals flickers
options.explanation: Silicon's melting point is the period's peak precisely because covalent bonds must break.

check.stem: In solid chlorine, which attraction breaks when the solid melts?

options.text: The weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between Cl2 molecules
options.explanation: Melting slides molecules past each other; the covalent bonds inside each molecule survive.

options.text: The covalent bond inside each Cl2 molecule
options.explanation: Intramolecular bonds persist through melting; boiling would still not break them.

options.text: Ionic bonds between chloride ions
options.explanation: No ions exist in molecular chlorine.

options.text: Metallic bonds in a chlorine lattice
options.explanation: Chlorine forms no metallic lattice.

check.stem: Which list correctly pairs each period-3 non-metal with its molecular form?

options.text: P4, S8, Cl2 and single-atom Ar
options.explanation: The four simple molecular species of the period's right-hand side.

options.text: P8, S4, Cl2 and diatomic Ar
options.explanation: The subscripts are swapped for phosphorus and sulfur, and argon is monatomic.

options.text: P2, S2, Cl8 and Ar8
options.explanation: None of these molecular sizes match the elements.

options.text: P4, S8, Cl8 and Ar2
options.explanation: Chlorine is diatomic and argon monatomic, not the reverse.

check.stem: State how many valence electrons each of Na, Mg and Al donates into the delocalised sea.
check.modelAnswer: Sodium donates one electron, magnesium two and aluminium three per atom.

check.stem: List the bonding and structural description of sodium and of silicon as given for the period-3 elements.
check.modelAnswer: Sodium is a giant metallic lattice of positive ions held by a sea of delocalised electrons; silicon is a giant molecular structure whose atoms are held to neighbours by strong covalent bonds.

check.stem: Explain why melting phosphorus or sulfur does not require breaking any covalent bond.
check.modelAnswer: Melting only disrupts the weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between neighbouring molecules; the strong covalent bonds inside each P4 or S8 unit remain intact until boiling or decomposition.

check.stem: Calculate how many delocalised electrons one mole of aluminium atoms supplies to the sea, using the Avogadro constant 6.02 x 10^23 mol^-1.
check.modelAnswer: Three electrons per atom times 6.02 x 10^23 atoms per mole gives 1.806 x 10^24 delocalised electrons per mole of aluminium.

glossary.definition: A regular array of positive ions held together by a sea of shared, delocalised valence electrons.
Valence electrons free to move through the whole metallic lattice rather than bound to one atom.
Describing elements that exist as small discrete molecules whose solids are bound only by weak intermolecular forces.

workedExample.prompt: How many delocalised electrons do 0.250 mol of magnesium atoms supply to the metallic sea?
steps: Magnesium donates two electrons per atom: 2 x 0.250 = 0.500 mol of electrons.
Convert to a count: 0.500 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 3.01 x 10^23 electrons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 0.250 mol of magnesium supplies 3.01 x 10^23 delocalised electrons.
